source_read: Saved PubMed Central page text (PMC6191498), read in full: abstract, all background sections, review aims, inclusion criteria and search approach, positive, negative and cognitive symptom sections, Tables 1–2 (as text), methodological limitations, summary and conclusions with the Figure 1 legend (the figure is an image), author contributions, conflict of interest and acknowledgments; reference list checked for the cited studies (140 entries).

anchors.locator: Positive symptoms › Acute meth psychosis vs. schizophrenia, 2nd paragraph; Table 1 rows 107, 110 and 111 (group sizes and instruments)
anchors.note: Data right as reconciled with Table 1: no positive-symptom difference by PANSS in Medhus et al. (9 vs 33) and Okada et al. (21 vs 14), by BPRS in Hides et al. (198 people who use methamphetamine), and by PANSS from admission to 12 months in Hajebi et al. The group sizes and the Hides result are in Table 1, not in the paragraph, and the paragraph itself cites PANSS for refs 110 and 117 and BPRS for ref 111 (Okada; PANSS in Table 1) without citing ref 107; card reporting issue 3 records the instrument mismatch.

anchors.locator: Table 1 row 105; Positive symptoms › Chronic; Negative symptoms › Chronic
anchors.note: Chen et al. (2015). The positive-symptom paragraph names the PANSS for this comparison, Table 1 and the negative-symptom paragraph the BPRS; the acute group was assessed about 9 weeks after its episode (Table 2; Positive symptoms › Chronic, 2nd paragraph), so its lower scores may partly reflect resolution.

anchors.locator: Methodological limitations and considerations, 1st and 3rd paragraphs; Table 1 rows 109 and 115 against Positive symptoms › Chronic meth psychosis vs. schizophrenia, 3rd and 1st paragraphs (editors' appraisal)
anchors.note: Factual basis confirmed: acute and persistent cases mixed (1st paragraph); small samples and uncontrolled medication (3rd paragraph); Wang et al. 53 vs 53 in Table 1 but 52 in the text; for McKetin et al. (2017), Table 1 has persistent above transient psychosis on visual, olfactory and tactile hallucinations, while the text says persistent and primary psychosis reported fewer visual and tactile hallucinations than transient psychosis.

for_senior_author: Risk of bias: re-appraised today by AI reader 3 with the editors' narrative-review checklist (overall high); reader 2's 'agree' was given to the superseded AMSTAR 2 rating. Domain judgments not re-judged here.
not_added: Reader 2's first missed item (ref. 140, Farnia et al., 2014) is already on the card as key finding 16, added by the editor in review round 1; checked here at the stated place (Summary and conclusions, 3rd paragraph; reference 140): confirmed, and the review reports no results of that trial. The editor's note on key finding 16 was left as it is.

Figures in cl_meth_psychosis_course that this review does not contain (16–17% at 1–3 months, the Thai cohort size, recurrence with renewed use): a claim matter; the review's own duration and transition figures are key findings 10 and 11.
